content: The University of Bradford Union (UBU) is managed by an executive team consisting of six full-time sabbatical officers, who are elected annually, and up to eleven part-time executive officers, who are elected every six months. Notably, the executive committee does not include a president, as the position was abolished in 2001 by Shumon Rahman, who had been elected as the Union's first Asian President in 2000. The structural reforms he introduced have remained in place since then. The executive team is overseen by a council of up to 40 elected students, who convene approximately six times per academic year. However, typically only 10 to 20 of these positions are filled at any given time, with co-option remaining open until all 40 seats are occupied. The Union operates from the Communal Building on campus and is known for its political activism, leaning nominally to the left, and for organizing regular campaigns. The Union provides two venues for nighttime events, named Escape and The Basement. Previously, it operated two bars, including the Biko Bar, located on the first floor of the Richmond Building and named after Steve Biko. However, the Biko Bar was closed in September 2005, and the space was repurposed into a new refectory following the construction of the university's atrium. The primary Student Union bar is now The Courtyard. The Union supports a wide range of student activities, with the most significant participation coming from sports clubs under the Athletics Association (commonly referred to as the AA) and various societies. Despite the university not offering performing arts courses until recently, there are several active music and theatre societies. The diversity of sports clubs is largely attributed to the centralized funding and membership structure of the AA, which provides support to smaller clubs. The Union's official colors are blue and red, although many sports teams continue to use their traditional black with red and white accents. The Union also operates Ramair, one of the UK's longest-running student radio stations, which broadcasts on 1350AM and online. Additionally, it publishes a student magazine called Kinetic and runs a film society and cinema, known as the Bradford Student Cinema, which screens professional 35mm films. The Union hosts an annual music festival called Infest, which takes place over the August bank holiday weekend. This festival features alternative electronic music acts and began in 1998 as a one-day event organized by three students and the Union's Entertainments Manager. It has since expanded into a three-day event. Ramair, the Union's student-run radio station, broadcasts locally on 1350AM and online. Its name originates from the Union's former logo, which featured a ram's head. Ramair is one of three media groups within the Union, alongside the Bradford Student Cinema and the student magazine. These media groups are not classified as sports clubs or societies but operate similarly to societies with memberships. However, because they provide services accessible to all students and staff, they fall under the jurisdiction of the Communications Officer. Ramair was established in 1980 and operates from two studios within the Union building. It is entirely run by student volunteers, who manage both the programming and technical aspects. Initially, the station broadcasted to students via induction loops in student halls, but this method proved unreliable. In the mid-1990s, a Low Power AM (LPAM) transmitter, affectionately named Doris, was installed in the car park of the former Shearbridge Halls, broadcasting on 1350AM with a maximum power of 1 watt. Ramair is also accessible online via an MP3 stream, allowing students to listen through the university's internet service and in various Union locations, such as the Union shop and laundrette. Most of Ramair's shows are broadcast in the evenings or on weekends when students are available. During the daytime, music is played from a computer system. Previously, the station syndicated content from the Student Broadcast Network (SBN) during off-hours, but this ceased in 2004 when SBN went bankrupt. Ramair's flagship program, Wednesday Night Sessions, features local music and acoustic performances by Bradford bands. The station also offers a variety of shows covering different music genres and news discussions. It plays a significant role in Union events, such as Freshers' Week, the May Carnival, and the end-of-year celebrations. During university breaks, the station broadcasts continuous music using a computer playout system. Ramair has achieved several milestones, including being the first student radio station to legally broadcast on FM. As of September 2007, it became the first student radio station accessible through Wii and PlayStation 3 browsers. In the past, it was also broadcast on 98FM via analogue cable television. Occasionally, Ramair broadcasts across the city of Bradford on an FM Restricted Service Licence (RSL), typically on 102FM, using a transmitter located atop the university's JB Priestley Library. The station also rents out its FM broadcast equipment to other student stations for their RSLs. Notable events include a live broadcast by Phill Jupitus for BBC 6 Music in April 2006, during which he interviewed Billy Bragg. One of Ramair's most famous former DJs is Lucio Buffone, who later won a Sony Award and now hosts a show on Capital Radio. The Bradford Student Cinema (BSC) is a film society that operates as part of the University of Bradford Union. It is one of the Union's three media groups, alongside Ramair and the student magazine. Like the other media groups, the BSC is not classified as a sports club or society but functions similarly to a society with membership. However, because it provides services accessible to all students and staff, it is overseen by the Communications Officer. The BSC is one of the Union's oldest societies, with its origins tracing back to the early days of the university. Formerly known as the Film Society, it initially screened 16mm films in lecture theatres within the Richmond Building. In 2000, the projection facilities in these lecture theatres were removed during renovations, and the society moved to the university's Great Hall, where it acquired a portable 35mm projection system. The Great Hall remains the venue for screenings and features what is believed to be the largest student cinema screen in the UK. The cinema's screen is a 9-meter-wide steel-framed structure with motorized adjustable masking. It is suspended from the roof and fills the proscenium arch of the Great Hall stage, creating a traditional cinema atmosphere. The projection box is located three floors above ground level, requiring the screen to be angled to eliminate keystoning. The balcony circle, which seats up to 337 people, is typically used for film showings due to the steep rake of the projector. In the mid-1990s, the BSC replaced its projector with a 1940s Westrex 2001 model, which remains in use today. In 2001, the Union funded an £8,500 upgrade to the cinema's projection facilities, including the installation of a Dolby CP55 processor, new amplifiers, speakers, and a subwoofer to enable surround sound. A red laser sound reader was also added to accommodate cyan soundtracks and improve sound quality. The lamphouse and rectifier were upgraded to support 2.5kW lamps. However, due to budget constraints, new surround speakers were not installed, and older speakers were repurposed for this function. In recent years, the BSC has hosted events such as the British Federation of Film Societies Student Group Conference and exclusive preview screenings in collaboration with the Daily Telegraph's Movie Mania Promotion. Like professional cinemas, it screens trailers and advertisements from Pearl & Dean. However, the BSC has faced challenges due to declining student numbers and competition from a 16-screen multiplex in Bradford city center. The Union has intervened to support the BSC, which now offers a reduced number of free screenings for staff and students throughout the academic year. In 2002, the BSC nominated actor Brian Blessed for an Honorary Doctor of Letters degree, which he received in 2003. Previously, cinema-goers could purchase drinks and snacks, including alcohol, at the Biko Bar in the Richmond Building, but this bar was closed in 2005. The cinema's operations have also been affected by the construction of a new £5.3 million atrium and front entrance, which opened in October 2006 to mark the university's 40th anniversary. Further delays have been caused by the refurbishment of the Great Hall, which began in January 2007. Despite these challenges, there are plans to resume regular screenings and to install a digital cinema projector alongside the existing 35mm facilities.
